items.prompt: What is the layer of feathers covering a bird called?

options.label: Feather coat
options.feedback: A coat is not the term used in bird science. The correct name for the whole covering is plumage.

options.label: Plumage
options.feedback: Plumage, also called feathering, is the entire layer of feathers and their pattern and colour.

options.label: Pelage
options.feedback: Pelage is the hair covering of mammals, not the feather covering of birds.

options.label: Down
options.feedback: Down is only one type of soft feather, not the whole covering. The full layer is called plumage.

items.ok_line: Yes, the whole feather covering is the plumage.
items.ko_line: That term does not name the full feather layer.
items.exp_text: Plumage, from the Latin word for feather, is the entire layer of feathers on a bird, including its pattern, colour, and arrangement.

items.prompt: How many times a year do most birds moult?

options.label: Once
options.feedback: Some birds, like many passerines, moult only once each year, but most birds moult twice, not once.

options.label: Three times
options.feedback: Three moults a year is not typical for most birds. Most moult twice annually.

options.label: Twice
options.feedback: Most birds moult twice a year, producing a breeding plumage and a non-breeding plumage.

options.label: Four times
options.feedback: Four moults a year is far more than typical. Most birds undergo two moults per year.

items.ok_line: Yes, most birds moult twice each year.
items.ko_line: The usual number of yearly moults is two.
items.exp_text: Most birds moult twice a year, replacing their feathers to form a breeding plumage and a non-breeding plumage.

items.prompt: What does a duck's eclipse plumage look like?

options.label: Dull and female-like
options.feedback: Correct. After breeding, many male ducks moult into a drab, cryptic plumage that resembles the female's.

options.label: Bright and colourful
options.feedback: Bright colours are the breeding plumage of male ducks, not the eclipse plumage. Eclipse is dull.

options.label: Pure white
options.feedback: White is not typical for eclipse plumage. Eclipse is a dull, brownish, female-like appearance.

options.label: Brighter than the breeding plumage
options.feedback: Eclipse plumage is duller, not brighter. The bright look is the breeding plumage.

items.ok_line: Yes, eclipse plumage is dull and resembles the female.
items.ko_line: Eclipse plumage is not bright or white.
items.exp_text: After breeding in mid-summer, many male ducks moult into a dull, female-like appearance called eclipse plumage, which helps them stay inconspicuous.

items.prompt: When a duck is in eclipse plumage, what happens to its flight feathers?

options.label: They turn white
options.feedback: The flight feathers do not change colour to white; they are shed all at once during eclipse.

options.label: They remain unchanged
options.feedback: In eclipse, ducks shed all their flight feathers simultaneously, so they do not remain unchanged.

options.label: They grow longer
options.feedback: The flight feathers are not growing longer; they are lost completely at once.

options.label: They are shed all at once
options.feedback: Ducks in eclipse shed all their flight feathers simultaneously, which makes them flightless for a short period.

items.ok_line: Yes, ducks lose all flight feathers at once in eclipse.
items.ko_line: The flight feathers are not kept, whitened, or lengthened.
items.exp_text: During eclipse, ducks shed all their flight feathers at the same time, so they become temporarily flightless.

items.prompt: Which bird group keeps its bright breeding plumage all year round?

options.label: Ducks
options.feedback: Ducks moult into a dull eclipse plumage after breeding, so they do not keep bright colours all year.

options.label: Hummingbirds
options.feedback: Male hummingbirds retain their bright plumage and show sexual dimorphism at all times, moulting only once a year.

options.label: Red junglefowl
options.feedback: Red junglefowl, like ducks, have an eclipse plumage after breeding, so they do not stay bright all year.

options.label: Fairywrens
options.feedback: Most fairywrens also have an eclipse plumage, so they do not keep breeding colours year-round.

items.ok_line: Yes, hummingbirds keep their bright plumage all year.
items.ko_line: That group moults into a duller plumage at some point.
items.exp_text: Unlike ducks, male hummingbirds and most lek-mating passerines keep their vivid plumage and sexual dimorphism all year, moulting only once annually.

items.prompt: What does colour polymorphism in a bird species mean?

options.label: The bird changes colour with the seasons
options.feedback: Seasonal colour change is a moult-related shift, not polymorphism. Polymorphism means different colour forms coexist in the population.

options.label: The bird has one fixed colour
options.feedback: A single fixed colour is not polymorphism, which requires two or more colour variants present at the same time.

options.label: Two or more colour variants occur in the population
options.feedback: Yes, in polymorphic species, both brown and grey morphs, for example, exist within the same population.

options.label: The bird loses all colour
options.feedback: Loss of all colour is albinism, not polymorphism. Polymorphism involves multiple colour forms, not absence.

items.ok_line: Yes, polymorphism means several colour variants coexist.
items.ko_line: Polymorphism is not a seasonal change or a single colour.
items.exp_text: In colour polymorphism, two or more colour variants, such as a brown and a grey morph, occur within the same bird population throughout most seasons.

items.prompt: Which bird has face colour polymorphism, with different coloured faces?

options.label: The red junglefowl
options.feedback: Red junglefowl are known for eclipse plumage, not for face colour polymorphism.

options.label: The Guianan cock-of-the-rock
options.feedback: The cock-of-the-rock keeps bright plumage all year; it is not known for face colour polymorphism.

options.label: The male ruff
options.feedback: The male ruff has different courtship types and neck colours, but the face colour example belongs to the Gouldian finch.

options.label: The Gouldian finch
options.feedback: The Gouldian finch shows unusual polymorphism in its face colour, with different colour variants in the population.

items.ok_line: Yes, the Gouldian finch has face colour polymorphism.
items.ko_line: That bird is not the example for face colour variants.
items.exp_text: The Gouldian finch is an example of a bird with polymorphism in its face colour, showing different colour forms within the same species.

items.prompt: What is the name for the total loss of colour in a bird?

options.label: Albinism
options.feedback: Albinism is the total loss of colour, a rare condition in birds.

options.label: Melanism
options.feedback: Melanism is an excess of dark colour, not a total loss of colour.

options.label: Leucism
options.feedback: Leucism is a loss of pigment in some or all feathers, not a total loss of colour in the whole bird.

options.label: Dilution
options.feedback: Dilution is a lower intensity of colour, not a complete absence of colour.

items.ok_line: Yes, total colour loss is albinism.
items.ko_line: That condition is different from total pigment loss.
items.exp_text: Albinism is the rare, total loss of colour in a bird, affecting feathers, eyes, bill, and skin due to a lack of melanin.

items.prompt: What causes the pink or red eyes of a completely albino bird?

options.label: A red pigment in the iris
options.feedback: There is no red pigment; the colour comes from blood showing through, not from a pigment.

options.label: A reflection of the sky
options.feedback: The eye colour is not a reflection; it is blood visible through a colourless iris.

options.label: Blood showing through the unpigmented iris
options.feedback: In a complete albino, the iris has no pigment, so the blood inside the eye makes it look pink or red.

options.label: A build-up of melanin
options.feedback: Melanin is absent in albinism, not built up; it cannot cause pink eyes.

items.ok_line: Yes, the blood shows through the clear iris.
items.ko_line: The pink colour is not due to any pigment.
items.exp_text: In a completely albino bird, the iris lacks pigment, so blood shows through, making the eyes appear pink or red.

items.prompt: What is the term for an overabundance of yellow pigment in a bird's feathers?

options.label: Melanism
options.feedback: Melanism is an excess of dark colour, not yellow. The yellow condition is xanthochromism.

options.label: Xanthochromism
options.feedback: Xanthochromism is an overabundance of yellow, a type of schizochroism in plumage.

options.label: Axanthism
options.feedback: Axanthism is a lack of yellow, not an overabundance of it.

options.label: Erythrism
options.feedback: Erythrism is an excess of reddish-brown pigment, not yellow.

items.ok_line: Yes, xanthochromism means too much yellow.
items.ko_line: That condition involves a different pigment imbalance.
items.exp_text: Xanthochromism is a colour shift where yellow pigments are overabundant in the feathers, one of the schizochroism conditions.
